1.problem: Call an ordered triple \((a, b, c)\) of integers feral if \(b-a\), \(c-a\), and \(c-b\) are all prime. Find the number of feral triples where \(1 \le a < b < c \le 20\).
1.solutions:
It’s essential to note that the pairs of twin primes in our range are \((3,5)\), \((5,7)\), \((11,13)\), \((17,19)\). The additional prime therein is 2.

If \(p_1, p_2\) are primes with \(|p_1-p_2|\) prime, then the correct ordering of \((k, k\pm p_1, k\pm p_2)\) is feral. If \(p_1+p_2\) is prime then the correct ordering of \((k, k\pm 2, k\mp p_1)\) is feral. The former condition is satisfied by the twin primes; the latter by 2 and the smaller in each pair of twin primes.

\[\begin{gathered} (k, k+3, k+5),\ 1\le k\le 15 \to 15 \qquad (k, k-3, k-5),\ 6\le k\le 20 \to 15\\ (k, k+5, k+7),\ 1\le k\le 13 \to 13 \qquad (k, k-5, k-7),\ 8\le k\le 20 \to 13\\ (k, k+11, k+13),\ 1\le k\le 7 \to 7 \qquad (k, k-11, k-13),\ 14\le k\le 20 \to 7\\ (k, k+17, k+19),\ 1\le k\le 1 \to 1 \qquad (k, k-17, k-19),\ 20\le k\le 20 \to 1 \end{gathered}\]

This gives a total of \(2(15+13+7+1)=\boxed{72}\).

We can see that there are no other solutions, since these are given by letting \(p_1=b-a\), \(p_2=c-a\), and \(a=k\), and that there is no double-counting.

2.problem: Let \(a\%b\) denote the remainder when \(a\) is divided by \(b\). Find \[\sum_{i=1}^{100}(100\%i).\]
2.solutions:
Note that \(100 = \lfloor \frac{100}{x} \rfloor x + 100\%x\). Therefore, if \(\frac{100}{n+1} < x \le \frac{100}{n}\), then \(100\%x = 100 - nx\).

Hence, we can split the initial sum into several smaller sums as follows: \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{100}(100\%i) &= \sum_{i=1}^{21}(100\%i) + \sum_{i=21}^{100}(100\%i)\\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{21}(100\%i) + 80\cdot 100 - \left(4\sum_{i=21}^{25} i + 3\sum_{i=26}^{33} i + 2\sum_{i=34}^{50} i + 1\sum_{i=51}^{100} i\right)\\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{21}(100\%i) + 8000 - (4\cdot 115 + 3\cdot 236 + 2\cdot 714 + 1\cdot 3775)\\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{21}(100\%i) + 1629. \end{aligned}\]

The sum from 1 to 21 can be evaluated directly to be 72, which makes the final answer \(\boxed{1701}\).

3.problem: Let \(f(x) = (x-5)(x-12)\) and \(g(x) = (x-6)(x-10)\). Find the sum of all integers \(n\) such that \(\frac{f(g(n))}{f(n)^2}\) is defined and an integer.
3.solutions:
Note that \[\begin{aligned} g(x) - 5 &= x^2 - 16x + 55 = (x-5)(x-11)\\ g(x) - 12 &= x^2 - 16x + 48 = (x-4)(x-12), \end{aligned}\] so that if \(h(n) = \frac{f(g(n))}{f(n)^2}\), then \[h(n) = \frac{(g(n)-5)(g(n)-12)}{(n-5)^2(n-12)^2} = \frac{(n-4)(n-11)}{(n-5)(n-12)}.\]

If \(n>12\), then \(n-5\) divides neither \(n-4\) nor \(n-11\), \(h(n)\) is not an integer. Similarly, if \(n<4\), then \(n-12\) divides neither \(n-4\) nor \(n-11\), so \(h(n)\) is still not an integer. Since \(h(5)\) and \(h(12)\) are undefined and \(h(4)=h(11)=0\), we only need to check \(h(6)\), \(h(7)\), \(h(8)\), \(h(9)\), and \(h(10)\), and it is clear that of these, only \(h(8)=1\) is an integer. Therefore, the answer is \(4+8+11=\boxed{23}\).

4.problem: Ayase chooses three numbers \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) independently and uniformly from the interval \([-1, 1]\). The probability that \(0 < a+b < a < a+b+c\) can be expressed in the form \(\frac{p}{q}\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are relatively prime positive integers. What is \(p+q\)?
4.solutions: \(0<a \Rightarrow a>0\), \(a+b<a \Rightarrow b<0\), and \(a+b<a+b+c \Rightarrow c>0\). Each of these conditions happens with probability \(\frac12\). Also, note that given \(a>0\) and \(b<0\), \(0<a+b \Rightarrow |a|>|b|\). Also, \(a+b+c>a \Rightarrow b+c>0 \Rightarrow |c|>|b|\). The probability that \(|b|\) is less than both \(|a|\) and \(|c|\) is \(\frac13\); consider ordering the 3 in a row. Hence, the final answer is \(\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac13=\frac{1}{24} \Rightarrow p+q=\boxed{25}\).

5.problem: Define the sequences \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) as follows: \(a_1 = 2017\) and \(b_1 = 1\). For \(n>1\), if there is a greatest integer \(k>1\) such that \(a_n\) is a perfect \(k\)th power, then \(a_{n+1} = \sqrt[k]{a_n}\); otherwise, \(a_{n+1} = a_n + b_n\). If \(a_{n+1} \ge a_n\) then \(b_{n+1} = b_n + 1\), otherwise \(b_{n+1} = b_n\). Find \(a_{2017}\).
5.solutions:
First, to understand what \(a_n\) looks like: each time the sequence resets, the difference between upcoming terms increases by one, so it will be an arithmetic sequence until that next reset.

We get the following table:

\[\begin{array}{c||c|c} n & a_n & b_n\\ \hline 1 & 2017 & 1\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\ 9 & 2025 & 1\\ 10 & 45 & 2\\ 11 & 47 & 2\\ 12 & 49 & 2\\ 13 & 7 & 3\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\ 16 & 16 & 3\\ 17 & 2 & 4\\ 18 & 6 & 4\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\ 2017 & \boxed{8002} & 4 \end{array}\]

The crucial step is to observe that, for \(n \ge 17\), \(a_n\) is always of form \(4k+2\); this cannot be a perfect power because \(4k+2 = 2(2k+1)\), which is always divisible by 2 but no greater integer power of 2.

6.problem: In regular pentagon \(ABCDE\), let \(O \in CE\) be the center of circle \(\Gamma\) tangent to \(DA\) and \(DE\). \(\Gamma\) meets \(DE\) at \(X\) and \(DA\) at \(Y\). Let the altitude from \(B\) meet \(CD\) at \(P\); if \(CP = 1\), the area of \(\triangle COY\) can be written in the form \(\frac{a}{b}\frac{\sin c^\circ}{\cos^2 c^\circ}\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are relatively prime positive integers and \(c\) is an integer in the range \((0, 90)\). Find \(a+b+c\).
6.solutions:
First, assume the pentagon has side length 1; at the end we will divide our value for \(\triangle COY\)’s area by \(CP^2\) (as area is quadratic in length). We note that \(\triangle COD\) is a \(36-54-90\) triangle, so \(CO=\frac{1}{\cos 36}\) and \(DO=\tan 36\). \(\triangle DOX\) is an \(18-72-90\) triangle so \(OX=OY=\sin 18\tan 36\).

Thus the desired area is, since \(\angle COY=18\), \(\frac12 CO\cdot OY\sin 18=\frac12\frac{\sin^2 18\sin 36}{\cos^2 36}\). \(\angle PCB=72\) so \(\angle PBC=18\) and thus \(PB=\sin 18\); the area now in the form \(\frac12\frac{\sin 36}{\cos^2 36}\) so the final answer is \(1+2+36=\boxed{39}\).

7.problem: 2017 voters vote by submitting a ranking of the integers \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 38\}\) from favorite (a vote for that value in 1st place) to least favorite (a vote for that value in 38th/last place). Let \(a_k\) be the integer that received the most \(k\)th place votes (the smallest such integer if there is a tie). Find the maximum possible value of \[\sum_{k=1}^{38} a_k.\]
7.solutions: Each number receives, on average, \(\frac{2017}{38}\approx 53.1\) votes in a given spot. Clearly 38 cannot be every entry on the composite ranking, because it can only be voted for 2017 times and by the pigeonhole principle it would have to get voted for at least 54 times each time it wins. However, it can win 36 times; that would account for 1944 votes. (It can’t win 37 times because while that would account for only 1998 votes, if it receives exactly 54 votes each time it wins and an extra vote 19 of those times there would be issues with the other numbers receiving exactly 53 votes, since \(53\cdot 37+54=2015\), so there would be two leftover votes each of those times. Allocating the extra 54 votes on top of the 18 would enable us to instead accomplish this, since a tie goes to the lower number.) We see that we now have ample room to award the two remaining spots in the composite ranking to 37, making our total \(38\cdot 36+37\cdot 2=\boxed{1442}\).

8.problem: Tristan is eating his favorite cereal, Tiger Crunch, which has marshmallows of two colors, black and orange. He eats the marshmallows by randomly choosing from those remaining one at a time, and he starts out with 17 orange and 5 black marshmallows. If \(\frac{p}{q}\) is the expected number of marshmallows remaining the instant that there is only one color left, and \(p\) and \(q\) are relatively prime positive integers, find \(p+q\).
8.solutions:
Suppose there are \(m\) orange and \(n\) black marshmallows. We compute the probability of there being exactly \(k\) marshmallows of a given color the instant that color is the only one remaining.

WLOG orange. First, we compute the probability of arriving at \(k\) orange and 1 black (this is the state right before our desired state); then we multiply by \(\frac{1}{k+1}\). We need to take \(m-k\) orange and \(n-1\) black marshmallows in some order. There are \(\binom{m+n-k-1}{m-k}\) ways to do this. We then multiply this by \(m(m-1)\cdots(k+1)=m!/k!\) the denominator of this probability, \(\frac{1}{m+n}\cdot\frac{1}{m+n-1}\cdots\frac{1}{k+2}=\frac{(k+1)!}{(m+n)!}\). This comes out with \(\frac{m!n!(k+1)!}{k!(m+n)!}\binom{m+n-k-1}{n-1}=(k+1)\frac{\binom{m+n-k-1}{n-1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}\). Multiplying by the probability of then choosing the last remaining black marshmallow gives \(\frac{\binom{m+n-k-1}{n-1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}\). The weight for the expectation is thus \(\frac{\binom{m+n-k-1}{n-1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}k\).

Using symmetry in the system to compute the case for black, we find \[\mathbb{E}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\binom{m+n-k-1}{n-1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}k+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\binom{m+n-k-1}{m-1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}k=\frac{1}{\binom{m+n}{m}}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{m}\binom{m+n-k-1}{n-1}k+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\binom{m+n-k-1}{m-1}k\right)\] and by the Hockey Stick Identity, \[\mathbb{E}=\frac{1}{\binom{m+n}{m}}\left(\binom{m+n}{n+1}+\binom{m+n}{m+1}\right)=\frac{m}{n+1}+\frac{n}{m+1}=\frac{28}{9},\] so the final answer is \(\boxed{37}\).

9.problem: The set \[\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid \lfloor x+y \rfloor \cdot \lceil x+y \rceil = (\lfloor x \rfloor + \lceil y \rceil)(\lceil x \rceil + \lfloor y \rfloor),\ 0 \le x, y \le 100\}\] can be thought of as a collection of line segments in the plane. If the total length of those line segments is \(a + b\sqrt{c}\) for \(c\) squarefree, find \(a+b+c\). (\(\lfloor z \rfloor\) is the greatest integer less than or equal to \(z\), and \(\lceil z \rceil\) is the least integer greater than or equal to \(z\), for \(z \in \mathbb{R}\).)
9.solutions:
Let \(n=100\). First, we will figure out what solutions to \(\lfloor x+y floor\cdot\lceil x+y ceil=(\lfloor x floor+\lceil y ceil)(\lceil x ceil+\lfloor y floor)\) look like in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Let \(\{z\}=z-\lfloor z floor\). Call \(a=\lfloor x floor\), \(b=\lfloor y floor\).

Case 1: \(\{x\} e0 e\{y\}\)

In this case, \(\lceil x ceil=a+1\) and \(\lceil y ceil=b+1\), so the right hand side becomes \((a+b+1)^2\). The multiplicands on the left differ by at most one and are in the range \([a+b,a+b+2]\), so they must both be \(a+b+1\); this means that \(x+y=a+b+1\), i.e. \(\{x\}+\{y\}=1\), or \(x+y\in\mathbb{Z}\).

Case 2a: \(\{x\}=0 e\{y\}\)

In this case, \(\lceil x ceil=a\) and \(\lceil y ceil=b+1\), so the right hand side becomes \((a+b)(a+b+1)\). The multiplicands on the left differ by at most one and are in the range \([a+b,a+b+2]\), so they must be \(a+b\) and \(a+b+1\). Therefore, any \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) is valid.

Case 2b: \(\{x\} e0=\{y\}\)

By symmetry with Case 2a, any \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) is valid.

Note that the case when \(\{x\}=0=\{y\}\) consists of isolated points, and so does not contribute any added length.

In the subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) consisting of points \((x,y)\) with \(0\le x,y\le n\), the solutions from Case 1 consist of diagonal segments satisfying \(x+y=k\) for integers \(1\le k\le 2n-1\) (minus some isolated points that do not affect the length). These have total length \[\sqrt2(1+2+\cdots+(n-1)+n+(n-1)+\cdots+2+1)=\sqrt2\left(2\cdot rac{n(n-1)}{2}+n ight)=n^2\sqrt2.\]

The solutions from Cases 2a and 2b consist of \((n+1)\) vertical segments and \((n+1)\) horizontal segments, respectively, each of which has length \(n\). The total length of these segments is \(2n(n+1)\), so the final length is \[2n(n+1)+n^2\sqrt2=20200+10000\sqrt2,\] which gives an answer of \( oxed{30202}\).

10.problem: Given a positive integer \(x \le 233\), let \(a\) be the remainder when \(x^{1943}\) is divided by \(233\). Find the sum of all possible values of \(a\).
10.solutions:
Observe that 233 is prime, so \(a^{232} \equiv 1 \pmod{233}\) for any \(a\). So \(x^{1943} = (x^{232})^8 \cdot x^{87} = x^{87} = (x^3)^{29}\). Furthermore, \(29 \cdot 8 = 232\), \((x^{87})^8 = 1\) for all \(x\), and the values of \(a\) correspond to solutions to \(a^8 \equiv 1 \pmod{233}\). For each solution, the negative of that solution is also a solution, so these 8 solutions come in four pairs, each of which sums to 233. Hence, the sum of all possible values of \(a\) is \(233 \cdot 4 = \boxed{932}\).

Problem written by Nathan Bergman

11.problem: For a sequence of 10 coin flips, each pair of consecutive flips and count the number of “Heads-Heads”, “Heads-Tails”, “Tails-Heads”, and “Tails-Tails” sequences is recorded. These four numbers are then multiplied to get the Tiger number of the sequence of flips. How many such sequences have a Tiger number of 24?
11.solutions:
Note that the number of “Heads-Tails” and “Tails-Heads” must be equal or differ by 1. So the possibilities for (number HH, number HT, number TH, number TT) are \((2,3,2,2)\), \((2,2,3,2)\), \((3,2,2,2)\) and \((2,2,2,3)\). The total number of sequences is then \(\boxed{180}\).

Problem written by Kai Zheng

12.problem: Call a positive integer \(n\) tubular if for any two distinct primes \(p\) and \(q\) dividing \(n\), \((p+q) \mid n\). Find the number of tubular numbers less than 100,000. (Integer powers of primes, including 1, 3, and 16, are not considered tubular.)
12.solutions:
Claim: all tubular numbers are divisible by \(2520 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7\).

Subclaim: 2 divides any tubular number. Suppose it doesn’t; then \(p, q \ne 2\) are primes dividing \(n\) that are both odd, so \(2 \mid (p+q) \mid n\).

Now, consider 2 and any odd prime \(p > 3\) dividing \(n\). \((p+2) \mid n\); either \(p+2\) is (an odd) prime, in which case \(p+2\) is composite, that composite value has a prime factor less than \(p' \le \sqrt{p+3 \pm 1} < p\), so \(p' \mid n\) and we have found a smaller odd prime factor of \(n\); we can continue to use descent until we reach \(3 \mid n \implies 5 \mid n \implies 7, 8 \mid n \implies 9 \mid n\), so combining all this gives \(2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7\). Call \(N = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7\).

Let’s say we want to construct a tubular number with a prime factor larger than 7, so we would have to multiply \(N\) by some other number \(k\). However, \(Nk \le 100000\) so \(k \le \lfloor 100000/N \rfloor = 39\). 11 is a reasonable place to start; however, this instantly entails \(11, 13 \mid k \implies 143 \mid k\). Trying 13 gives \(13, 15, 16, 18, 20 \mid n\), which is satisfied by \(n = 26N\). Trying 17 gives \(17, 19 \mid n \implies 323 \mid k\); comparable problems arise for the other primes less than 39 (23, 29, 31, 37). So, our values of \(k\) are restricted to those divisible by exclusively \(2, 3, 5, 7\), \(26\); there are in fact \(\boxed{26}\) such values.

Problem written by Zack Stier

13.problem: A point-sized cue ball is fired in a straight path from the center of a regular hexagonal billiards table of side length 1. If it is not launched directly into a pocket but travels an integer distance before falling into one of the pockets (located in the corners), find the minimum distance that it could have traveled.
13.solutions:
Consider the tiling of the plane with hexagons. This represents the possible reflections of the cue ball as it hits a wall – i.e. instead of reflecting the ball’s path about the wall, we reflect the table across the wall and continue the path straight. Thus the following argument will get us our answer.

The cue ball starts at the origin; let \(C_n = (0, n\sqrt3)\) and \(v = \left(\frac12, \frac12\sqrt3\right)\). We restrict our consideration to a sixth of the plane: the sector swept out by the positive \(y\)-axis rotated clockwise by \(60^\circ\). The rest of the plane is just 5 other copies of this sector, rotated by some multiple of \(60^\circ\). We wish to find points here that are an integer distance from the origin. These occur at \(H_{n,k} = C_n + kv\) for \(3 \nmid k\) but otherwise \(n, k \in \mathbb{N}\). Thus, \(H_{n,k} = \left(\frac12 k, \left(n+\frac12 k\right)\sqrt3\right)\) and its magnitude is \(\sqrt{3n^2+3nk+k^2}\). We now search for the minimal integer value that this can take. For \(k=1\) we need to find integer values of \(\sqrt{3n^2+3n+1} = \frac12\sqrt{3(2n+1)^2+1}\); computation gives that this first occurs at \(n=7\). For \(k=2\) we need to find integer values of \(\sqrt{3n^2+6n+4} = \sqrt{3(n+1)^2+1}\); computation gives that this occurs at \(n=3\), an improvement. For \(k=4\) we need to find integer values of \(\sqrt{3n^2+12n+16} = \sqrt{3(n+2)^2+4}\); computation gives that this occurs at \(n=6\), worse than \(H_{3,2}\). After seeing that nothing close to \(H_{3,2}\) works for \(k=5\) we can rule out anything larger because that will have \(k^2 > 3\cdot3^2+2^2\). Thus, \(\|H_{3,2}\| = \boxed{7}\) is our final answer.

Problem written by Zack Stier

14.problem: Eric rolls a ten-sided die (with sides labeled 1 through 10) repeatedly until it lands on 3, 5, or 7. Conditional on all of Eric’s rolls being odd, the expected number of rolls can be expressed as \(\frac{m}{n}\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are relatively prime positive integers. Compute \(m+n\).
14.solutions:
If you got \(\frac53\), consider yourself trolled. You cannot simply assume that you have a five-sided die (with just the odd numbers) and calculate the expected number of rolls until you roll a 3, 5, or 7. An intuitive way to realize this is that short sequences of rolls are particularly likely because the longer the roll, the likelier it is that at some point you’ll roll an even number.

Instead, we use the identity \(\Pr[A \mid B]\Pr[B] = \Pr[B \mid A]\Pr[A]\) (known as Bayes’s theorem). Specifically we have the following: \[\Pr[\text{length}=k \mid \text{all odd}]\Pr[\text{all odd}] = \Pr[\text{all odd} \mid \text{length}=k]\Pr[\text{length}=k].\]

We wish to know the first probability above as part of computing the expected value. The second probability is easily computed: it is \(\frac{3}{10}+\frac{2}{10}\cdot\frac{3}{10}+\left(\frac{2}{10}\right)^2\cdot\frac{3}{10}+\cdots = \frac38\). The second probability is \(\frac{2^{k-1}\cdot3}{7^{k-1}\cdot3} = \left(\frac27\right)^{k-1}\), because there are \(2^{k-1}\cdot3\) ways to roll the dice so that all rolls are odd and only the last roll is 3, 5, or 7, and \(7^{k-1}\cdot3\) total ways to roll the dice so that only the last roll is 3, 5, or 7. The third probability is \(\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{k-1}\cdot\frac{3}{10}\) since a sequence of rolls has length \(k\) if and only if the first \(k-1\) rolls are not 3, 5, or 7 and the last roll is 3, 5, or 7.

This gives us \[\Pr[\text{length}=k \mid \text{all odd}] = \frac83\cdot\left(\frac27\right)^{k-1}\cdot\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{k-1}\cdot\frac{3}{10} = \frac{4}{5^k}.\]

Thus, the answer is \[\frac45\cdot1+\frac{4}{25}\cdot2+\frac{4}{125}\cdot3+\cdots.\]

We can write this as \(\left(\frac45+\frac{4}{25}+\cdots\right)+\left(\frac{4}{25}+\frac{4}{125}+\cdots\right)+\cdots\). The geometric series formula tells us that the parenthetical values are, respectively, \(1\), \(\frac15\), \(\frac{1}{25}\), and so on, and using the geometric series formula once more gives us a final answer of \(\frac54\). Therefore, we have \(m+n=\boxed{9}\).

Problem written by Eric Neyman; inspired by Elchanan Mossel

15.problem: How many ordered pairs of positive integers \((x, y)\) satisfy \(yx^y = y^{2017}\)?
15.solutions:
Given \(yx^y=y^{2017}\), we can rewrite this to obtain \(x^y=y^{2016} \implies x=y^{2016/y}\). Therefore, we want to find positive integer values of \(y\) that make the quantity \(y^{2016/y}\) an integer. We can split the potential solutions for \(y\) into 2 sets: where \(\frac{2016}{y}\) is an integer, and where it is not. The first set is simple; the prime factorization of 2016 is \(2^5\cdot3^2\cdot7\), so there are \(6\cdot3\cdot2=36\) factors of 2016, each of which generates a unique, valid solution \((x,y)\). The second set can be computed as follows: let \(y=kd\), where \(d\) is a (maximal) divisor of 2016 and \(y\) is not a divisor of 2016. Then, \((kd)^{2016/kd}=\left((kd)^{1/k}\right)^{2016/d}\). A sufficient condition for this quantity to be an integer is that \(kd\) is a perfect \(k^{\text{th}}\) power, so that \((kd)^{1/k}\) can be an integer.

  • If \(k=2\), and since \(kd\) is not a factor of 2016, we need \(d=2^5\cdot n\), where \(n\) is a perfect square factor, namely either 1 or \(3^2\), yielding 2 solutions.
  • If \(k=3\), we need \(d=3^2\cdot n\), where \(n\) is a perfect cube factor, namely either 1 or \(2^3\), yielding 2 solutions.
  • If \(k=4,5,6\), or 7, there are no solutions.
  • If \(k=8\), we need \(2^3\cdot n\) to be a perfect \(8^{\text{th}}\) power, namely \(n=2^5\) is the only possible, yielding 1 more.

This yields a total of \(36+5=\boxed{41}\) solutions.

Problem written by Jackson Blitz; solution written by Juneseo Lee

16.problem: Robert is a robot who can move freely on the unit circle and its interior, but is attached to the origin by a retractable cord such that at any moment the cord lies in a straight line connecting Robert to the origin. Whenever his movement is counterclockwise (relative to the origin), the cord leaves a coating of black paint on the ground, and whenever his movement is clockwise, the cord leaves a coating of orange paint on the ground. The paint is dispensed regardless of whether there is already paint on the ground. The paints covers 1 gallon/unit\(^2\), and Robert starts at \((1,0)\). Each second, he moves in a straight line from the point \((\cos(\theta), \sin(\theta))\) to the point \((\cos(\theta+\alpha), \sin(\theta+\alpha))\), where \(\alpha\) changes after each movement. \(\alpha\) starts out as \(253^\circ\) and decreases by \(2^\circ\) each step. If he takes 89 steps, then the difference, in gallons, between the amount of black paint used and orange paint used can be written as \(\frac{\sqrt a-\sqrt b}{c}\cot 1^\circ\), where \(a, b, c\) are positive integers and no prime divisor of \(c\) divides both \(a\) and \(b\) twice. Find \(a+b+c\).
16.solutions:
The black paint covers the area \(\sum_{0\le\theta<\pi}|\sin\theta|\) and the orange paint covers the area \(\sum_{\pi\le\theta<2\pi}|\sin\theta|\). The difference is thus actually equal to \(\sum_\theta\sin\theta\), where these values of \(\theta\) are the angles pivoted by Robert. \(\theta(k) = (253-2k)^\circ\) for \(0\le k<89\). Thus we wish to compute \(\sum_{k=0}^{88}\sin(253-2k)^\circ = \sum_{k=0}^{88}\sin(88+164-2k+1)^\circ\). Let \(m=88, n=164, \theta=1^\circ\). We wish to evaluate \(\sum_{k=0}^m\sin((m+n-2k+1)\theta) = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\sum_{k=0}^m\sin((m+n-2k+1)\theta)\sin\theta\). Use the product-to-sum rule to obtain a telescoping series; use the sum-to-product rule after collapsing the telescope to see that the sum equals \(\frac{\sin((m+1)\theta)\sin((n+1)\theta)}{\sin\theta}\). Using our values, this is equal to \(\sin15^\circ\cot1^\circ = \frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\cot1^\circ\). Thus our answer is \(6+2+4=\boxed{12}\).

Problem written by Zack Stier and Matt Tyler

17.problem: Zack keeps cutting the interval \([0,1]\) of the number line, each time cutting at a uniformly random point in the interval, until the interval is cut into pieces, none of which have length greater than \(\frac35\). The expected number of cuts that Zack makes can be written as \(\frac{p}{q}\) for \(p\) and \(q\) relatively prime positive integers. Find \(p+q\).
17.solutions:
We wish to compute \(\mathbb{E}=1\cdot\mathbb{P}[1]+2\cdot\mathbb{P}[2]+\cdots\), where \(\mathbb{P}[n]\) is the probability that exactly \(n\) points were necessary for none of the gaps to be greater than \(\frac35\) and \(n-1\) were insufficient. We can rewrite this as \(\mathbb{E}=\mathbb{P}[\ge1]+\mathbb{P}[\ge2]+\cdots\) where \(\mathbb{P}[\ge n]\) is the probability that at least \(n\) points were necessary for none of the gaps to be greater than \(\frac35\) and \(n-1\) were insufficient.

Fix \(n\) and let \(a\) be the rightmost value to the left of the \(\frac35\)-length gap among the first \(n-1\) points selected (we know there is only one because \(2\cdot\frac35>1\)). We look to evaluate the probability that the \(n\)th point lies – if that were the case, it would lie in some small neighborhood to the right of \(a\), of length \(da\). If there are \(k-1\) points to the left of \(a\) there are \(n-k\) to the right; so we find that this occurs with probability \(\binom{n-1}{k-1}a^{k-1}\left(1-\left(a+\frac35\right)\right)^{n-k}n\,da\) (the factor of \(n\) comes from symmetry – this argument could apply to any of the \(n\) points). Summing gets \(\sum_{k=1}^n\binom{n-1}{k-1}a^{k-1}\left(1-\left(a+\frac35\right)\right)^{n-k}n\,da = n\left(1-\frac35\right)^{n-1}da\) and adding up over all possible values of \(a\) gets the rudimentary integral (since the integrand is in fact a constant in \(a\)) \(\int_0^{1-\frac35}n\left(1-\frac35\right)^{n-1}da=n\left(1-\frac35\right)^n\). We add in another \(\left(1-\frac35\right)^n\) to account for the case in which all \(n-1\) points lie to the right. This gets \(\mathbb{P}[\ge n]=(n+1)\left(1-\frac35\right)^n\). Thus: \[\mathbb{E}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)\left(1-\frac35\right)^n=\frac{1}{\left(\frac35\right)^2}=\frac{25}{9}\] so our final answer is \(\boxed{34}\).
